name: Mewing pseudoscience critique

lead: Mewing is a tongue-posture practice that people use hoping to sharpen the jawline and improve facial structure. The critique of mewing is the collected position of orthodontists, surgeons and researchers who say the claim that posture reshapes adult facial bones has not been demonstrated.

Critics point out that orthotropics, the theory behind mewing, has no clinical trial showing it changes jaw structure, and that professional bodies such as the American Association of Orthodontists say there is no evidence it improves the jaw. Proponents answer that anecdotal before-and-after photos and the theory of oral posture shaping growth support it, and that rigorous studies have simply not been done.

paras: People who read the critique typically use it to compare mewing with other routes to a stronger-looking jaw, such as body-fat reduction, orthodontic or surgical consultation, and dental care. Practitioners of mewing generally continue to describe resting the tongue against the palate, often alongside nasal breathing and good head posture.

Critics have raised concerns mainly about children treated with Mew's appliance-based orthotropic approach, which was the subject of a UK tribunal, and about the time and expectations invested in a method that has not been shown to work. Forceful pressing (often called hard mewing) is discussed by some clinicians as a possible source of jaw or tooth discomfort.

angle.text: The critique documents what professional bodies and researchers say about mewing's ability to change facial structure. People use it to decide how mewing fits alongside other approaches to the jaw, such as leaning out, dental or orthodontic care, or surgery.

lead: The mewing pseudoscience critique is the set of objections from orthodontists, oral surgeons and researchers to mewing, a tongue-posture practice that people use in the hope of improving the look of the jawline, chin and midface. Mewing is named after British orthodontist John Mew, who developed the theory of orthotropics together with his son Mike Mew.[1] Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven form of oral posture training and labels it pseudoscientific.[1]

The central claim of mewing is that resting the tongue on the roof of the mouth and applying pressure can modify jaw and facial structure.[1] Critics say no credible published research has shown that orthotropics is effective, and that most orthodontists do not regard it as an alternative to orthognathic (jaw) surgery.[1] The American Association of Orthodontists has stated that there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw, and published an explainer on the subject in March 2025.[1]

Two articles in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, in 2019 and 2021, discussed mewing and similar social-media trends in the context of cosmetic surgery practice.[1] Practitioners and fans of mewing, for their part, point to personal photo comparisons and to the broader idea that oral posture influences growth, and many say they continue because they see changes in how their face looks.
infobox: AAO states no evidence mewing improves the jaw[1]

paras: Orthotropics is the theory, developed by John Mew, that facial growth can be guided by posture of the tongue and mouth.[1] The term mewing came from his name and spread widely online, with Google Trends interest rising from January 2019.[1] The Guardian covered it as a YouTube craze in March 2019, and The New York Times Magazine reported in August 2020 on orthodontists who had gained a following among online male communities.[1]

Critics make three broad points. First, that no credible research has demonstrated that orthotropics changes facial structure.[1] Second, that the AAO and most orthodontists say there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw and do not treat it as an alternative to surgery.[1] Third, that results shown online may reflect age, weight change, lighting, angle or lens rather than bone change; this is a point commonly raised by clinicians, though the sources loaded here do not attribute it to a specific study.

Supporters respond that adult tongue posture has not been studied in controlled trials precisely because it is unfunded, that growth in children is influenced by function, and that their own photographs show change.

Mike Mew was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society and faced a misconduct hearing over alleged harm to child patients, reported from 2022 to 2023, and was struck off the UK dental register in 2024.[1] The BBC reported in April 2023 on a boy with seizure-like episodes linked to treatment.[1]
No studies found. Commentary articles in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery (2019, 2021) discuss mewing as a social-media trend but are opinion pieces rather than trials of its effect.[1]

Mewing became one of the best-known terms in looksmaxxing, and press coverage in 2023 and 2024 tied it to looksmaxxing and incel subcultures and to schoolroom disruption, with The Independent reporting teachers pushing back in March 2024.[1]
